opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at the beginning I wasn't thinking about data at all. During my PhD at Caltech, working with Pietro Perona, the field was really focused on models. Everyone was asking: what's the right algorithm, the right features, the right Bayesian framework? Data was almost an afterthought. You'd collect a few hundred images, maybe a handful of categories, and test your model on that.

In fact, some of my early work went in the opposite direction. We were interested in what we called one-shot learning: how can a system learn a new object category from just one or a few examples, the way humans seem to? That was inspired by cognitive science, and it was a beautiful question. But along the way we built Caltech 101, a dataset of 101 object categories, which at the time felt big. And I started to notice something: models were overfitting, they weren't generalizing, and no amount of clever tweaking seemed to get us past that.

The real shift came from thinking about how children learn. A young child sees an enormous number of images of the world, a continuous stream of experience, hundreds of millions of "frames" in the first few years. And I came across Irving Biederman's estimate that humans can recognize on the order of tens of thousands of object categories. So I thought: we're trying to solve visual intelligence with a tiny fraction of the experience any human has. Maybe the bottleneck isn't only the model. Maybe it's the data.

That led to the hypothesis behind ImageNet: that you need data at the scale and diversity of the real world. Building on WordNet's structure, we aimed for tens of thousands of categories and millions of images. A lot of people thought it was crazy, or at least not "real research." But I really believed that data could drive the models, rather than just serve as a test set at the end. And in hindsight, that turned out to be one of the key ingredients, together with neural networks and GPUs, in what became the deep learning revolution.

r002.rationale: It says models were overfitting and not generalizing, then identifies real-world-scale, diverse data as the needed change.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, when I was doing my PhD at Caltech in the early 2000s, the whole field had a very different relationship with data than it does now. The dominant way of thinking was that the algorithm was the thing. You'd pick a handful of object categories, maybe a few hundred images each, and the intellectual work was in designing the model, the features, the probabilistic structure. Data was almost an afterthought, something you collected just enough of to run your experiments.

But I kept running into this wall. We'd build these elaborate generative models, and they would work on the training set, and then the moment you showed them a slightly different view of a cat or a bicycle, they fell apart. And I started asking myself a question that felt almost naive at the time: how does a child do this? A child sees the world at something like thirty frames a second, for years, and nobody hands them a carefully curated dataset. The sheer quantity of visual experience is staggering.

That reframing really changed how I thought about the problem. I started to believe that we had the ratio backwards. We were spending ninety percent of our effort on the algorithm and ten percent on the data, and maybe the real bottleneck was that our models had simply never seen enough of the world to learn anything general. One of my earlier projects during that period was actually about one-shot learning, learning a category from very few examples, and even there the lesson was that you could only do it if the model had already been exposed to a lot of other categories first. The prior knowledge had to come from somewhere, and it came from scale.

So by the end of my PhD, the conviction was forming that if we wanted machines to recognize objects the way humans do, we needed to think about data at a scale that nobody in the field was taking seriously. Not hundreds of images, not thousands, but millions, across thousands of categories. That idea felt a little reckless when I first said it out loud to people. But it was really the seed of what later became ImageNet.

r001.rationale: The response says the field underestimated data and that Li came to believe more data was needed, but it does not state that around 2003 she and her collaborators did not know how far more training data could improve recognition.

r002.rationale: It says the models had not seen enough of the world to learn anything general, directly identifying generalization as a reason to seek more data.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe selecting categories using illustrated words in a dictionary.

astra-6.text:
During my PhD, I was thinking about how we could get machines to learn objects from very few examples. Humans can see something once or twice and recognize it again, so that seemed like an important problem to work on.

But there’s a tension there: a child who learns a new object from one example has already had years of visual experience. That one example isn’t the entirety of the data they’ve seen. So the question gradually became, what kind of visual experience does a machine need before it can learn and recognize things reliably? That pushed my thinking toward the importance of data—not just the number of images, but the diversity of the visual world those images represent.

sol-6.1.text:
During my PhD, I was fascinated by how humans recognize objects. We can see a new object just a few times and learn something meaningful about it. So one question I worked on was whether a machine could also learn from very few examples.

But there’s a distinction between how many examples you need to learn a new category and how much visual experience you need to build a visual system in the first place. By the time a child learns the name of an animal, they’ve already had an enormous amount of visual experience.

That became a very important shift in my thinking. We were putting so much attention into models and algorithms, but the data we gave them captured such a small slice of the visual world. If we wanted object recognition to work beyond a few carefully chosen categories, we needed data that reflected much more of that world’s richness and diversity.

r002.rationale: It says more diverse data was needed for object recognition to work beyond a few carefully chosen categories, communicating the goal of generalizing beyond limited categories.
